topic: Buyer oversight on a cost-plus contract
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Artifacts (4.6.8): agreements and contracts — who carries cost risk under cost-reimbursable terms
question: A county transit agency hired an engineering firm under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract to design a first-of-its-kind battery-charging depot, because the technical scope could not be defined well enough to price. Four months in, the firm's monthly invoices are running 35% above its original cost estimate, and the latest invoice includes hours charged for staff who worked on another client's proposal. The agency's contracting officer asks the project manager for a recommendation. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Audit the invoices against the contract's allowable-cost terms and tighten cost reporting, since the agency bears the overrun risk
Convert the agreement to a firm fixed price now, so that the engineering firm absorbs any further growth in its design costs from here on
Pay the invoices as submitted, because a cost-plus contract entitles the seller to recover all of the costs it incurs
Withhold the fixed fee until the design is finished, to give the firm a strong financial reason to control its costs
hint: Under this contract type, whose money is at risk when costs grow, and what does that party therefore have to do?
why: In a cost-reimbursable contract the buyer pays the seller's actual allowable costs plus a fee, so the buyer carries most of the cost risk. That makes buyer-side oversight essential: checking invoices against the contract's allowable-cost terms, questioning charges that do not belong to this work (such as time spent on another client's proposal), and requiring regular cost reporting and forecasts. Changing the contract type mid-stream or withholding the fee are not the agency's to impose unilaterally.
how: Match your contract oversight to who carries the risk: under cost-reimbursable contracts the buyer must verify allowable costs and watch spending closely; under fixed-price contracts the buyer's focus shifts to scope clarity and acceptance.
optionNotes: Correct — The buyer bears the cost risk under cost-plus terms, so auditing allowability and tightening cost reporting is the right protective step.
Incorrect — Scope is still undefined, so a fixed price would need renegotiation, carry a large risk premium, and cannot be imposed by the buyer alone.
Incorrect — Only allowable, properly documented costs for this contract are reimbursable; time spent on another client's proposal is not.
Incorrect — The fixed fee is owed under the agreed terms; withholding it unilaterally risks a breach and a claim, and does not address the invalid charges.
deepDive: Contract types spread risk differently: firm fixed price places most cost risk on the seller, fixed-price incentive and economic-price-adjustment variants share some, and cost-reimbursable types (cost plus fixed fee, incentive fee, award fee) place most of it on the buyer. The book notes that cost-reimbursable contracts fit work whose scope is not well defined or changes often, which is why the agency chose one here. The trade-off is that the buyer needs the capacity to audit costs, set ceilings or not-to-exceed limits, and track forecasts. A common exam trap is assuming 'cost plus' means the buyer pays anything invoiced; only allowable, reasonable and allocable costs qualify.

topic: Scope swaps under an agile contract
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 5 · Agile contracting (swap clause versus contract amendment)
question: A software vendor is building a mobile banking app for a credit union under a fixed-budget agile contract. The contract lets the client exchange not-yet-started backlog items for new items of equal estimated size at no charge; anything beyond that requires a written contract amendment. Midway through, the credit union's product owner asks the vendor team to add a 40-point budgeting feature while keeping every existing item. The vendor's account manager tells the project manager to 'just absorb it' to keep the client happy. What should the project manager do?
options: Absorb the feature quietly by asking the team to raise its velocity, so that the relationship with the client stays positive
Decline the feature, because the budget and the scope were both fixed at signing, and suggest raising it again next year
Explain the swap option to the product owner and, if nothing can be removed, route the added scope through an amendment
Add the feature to the backlog now and bill the extra sprints later at time-and-materials rates once its value is clear
hint: Before deciding who pays, check what mechanism the agreement itself already provides for this kind of change.
why: The contract gives two routes: swap equal-sized, unstarted items at no cost, or amend the contract for added scope. Laying out both routes lets the product owner decide what matters most, keeps the relationship transparent, and follows the terms both parties signed. Absorbing 40 unfunded points hides a real cost, pressures the team and sets a precedent; refusing ignores the flexibility the contract deliberately built in; billing later without an amendment is a unilateral change that damages trust.
how: When an agile contract defines how scope may change, use that mechanism openly: offer the no-cost option first (trade equal-value work), and use formal contract change control for genuine additions.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Absorbing unfunded scope hides the real cost, pressures the team into unsustainable pace, and invites further unmanaged scope creep.
Incorrect — The contract deliberately allows equal-size swaps, so a flat refusal ignores flexibility the client is entitled to and harms collaboration.
Correct — It follows the agreed change mechanism, gives the product owner a value-based choice, and handles genuine additions through a formal amendment.
Incorrect — Billing later at different rates without a signed amendment is a unilateral contract change and is likely to end in a dispute.
deepDive: Agile contracts often fix budget and timeline while letting scope flex, sometimes with a 'change for free' clause that allows swapping items of equal size, and an early-termination option. The book's view of procurement stresses that contracts should support collaboration, but they remain binding: changes beyond the agreed flexibility need formal amendment. On the exam, watch for options that quietly absorb scope (gold plating for the client) or that bill without authority; both skip change control. The PMI-aligned answer is transparent, uses the agreement, and keeps the product owner in charge of priorities.

topic: Drawing on reserves and the baseline
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Planning Performance Domain (2.4.2.4): budget — contingency reserve versus management reserve
question: A hospital wing renovation has work package estimates totaling $1,500,000. The approved cost baseline also includes a $120,000 contingency reserve for risks in the risk register, and the sponsor holds an $80,000 management reserve. During construction, a registered risk (asbestos behind old walls) occurs and costs $45,000 to resolve. Later, an unforeseen fire-code change that no one had identified adds $30,000 of work, and the sponsor approves funding it from management reserve through change control. After both events are handled correctly, what is the cost baseline?
hint: Ask which reserve sits inside the baseline and which sits outside it, and which kind of risk each one is meant to fund.
why: The original cost baseline is $1,500,000 + $120,000 contingency = $1,620,000 (budget = $1,620,000 + $80,000 = $1,700,000). The asbestos risk was identified, so its $45,000 comes out of contingency that is already inside the baseline, leaving $75,000 of contingency and the baseline unchanged. The fire-code change was unidentified, so the approved $30,000 moves from management reserve into the baseline: $1,620,000 + $30,000 = $1,650,000 (management reserve drops to $50,000, and the total budget stays $1,700,000).
how: Contingency reserve (known-unknowns) is inside the cost baseline, so using it does not change the baseline; management reserve (unknown-unknowns) is outside the baseline, so using it requires approval and increases the baseline.
optionNotes: Incorrect — This is the original baseline; it ignores that approved management reserve funding for the fire-code work is added to the baseline.
Correct — The asbestos cost is absorbed by contingency inside the baseline, and only the $30,000 released from management reserve raises it.
Incorrect — This adds the $45,000 contingency draw as well, but contingency is already part of the baseline, so it is counted twice.
Incorrect — This is the total project budget (baseline plus the full management reserve), not the cost baseline after the approved change.
deepDive: Layering: activity and work package estimates roll up with contingency reserves into the cost baseline; adding management reserve gives the project budget. The book frames contingency as money set aside for identified risks the team chooses to accept, and management reserve as money for unforeseen work within scope, usually controlled by the sponsor or governance body. Earned value is measured against the cost baseline, so moving management reserve into it must be a formal, approved change. A classic exam trap is to treat any reserve draw as a baseline change or to confuse the baseline with the total budget.

topic: Agile scope versus a funding cut
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 6 · Agile practice (fixed cost per sprint, flexible scope)
question: An eight-person agile team is building an online permit application portal for a city. Its cost is essentially fixed at $48,000 per two-week sprint, and the annual plan funded 20 more sprints. The finance office has just announced a mid-year cut that leaves funding for only 15 of those sprints. The sponsor still wants a usable portal launched this year. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Work with the product owner to reprioritize the backlog so the most valuable features fit within the 15 funded sprints
Ask the team to raise its velocity by about a third, so that all of the planned scope still fits within the 15 funded sprints
Keep the current release plan and submit an exception request to restore the funding for the five lost sprints
Drop automated testing from the definition of done, so that more features can be finished in each funded sprint
hint: With a stable team, cost per sprint barely moves — so which of the constraints can actually flex?
why: A stable agile team's cost per sprint is effectively fixed, so a funding cut becomes a cut in the number of sprints; what can flex is scope. The first step is to re-plan with the product owner, ordering the backlog so the highest-value, usable features fit the 15 funded sprints, and then share the revised forecast with the sponsor. Demanding more velocity or weakening quality only hides the gap, and asking for an exception before understanding the impact skips the analysis the sponsor needs.
how: When funding is reduced on an agile effort, hold the team and quality steady, flex scope through backlog prioritization with the product owner, and give stakeholders an updated value-based forecast.
optionNotes: Correct — Scope is the variable in a fixed-cost team; reprioritizing with the product owner keeps the most valuable, usable features within the new funding limit.
Incorrect — Velocity is an outcome of capacity, not a lever; demanding a one-third jump invites inflated estimates, burnout, and hidden quality problems.
Incorrect — Requesting more money may be reasonable later, but doing it first skips the impact analysis and ignores the new funding constraint.
Incorrect — Weakening the definition of done trades a short-term gain for defects and technical debt, undermining quality built into the product.
deepDive: Funding limit reconciliation means aligning planned spending with the money actually available, which in predictive work often means rescheduling activities through change control. In agile work with a stable team, the 'iron triangle' is inverted: cost and time are fixed per sprint, and scope is adjusted to fit. The product owner owns value ordering, so reprioritization goes through them, and release forecasts are updated for stakeholders. Exam traps include demanding higher velocity, cutting quality practices, or escalating before analyzing the impact.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.3): quality — process stability and assignable causes
question: Refer to the exhibit. A project is commissioning a new sauce-bottling line, and the acceptance criteria require the fill process to be stable before handover. The quality engineer traced the point above the upper control limit at sample 5 to a scale that was out of calibration, and the scale was recalibrated the same day. The line supervisor now says the process is stable because no other point is outside the limits. What should the project manager conclude?
options: The process is stable, because the only point outside the limits has a known cause that has already been corrected
The control limits are too tight for a new line, so they should be widened before the handover review takes place
Operators should adjust the filler after each low reading, so that the sample mean moves back toward 500 grams
The run of low samples since sample 9 signals a likely assignable cause that needs investigating before handover
hint: Being inside the limits is not the only test of a stable process — look for patterns as well as single points.
why: Samples 9 through 15 all fall below the mean: seven consecutive points on one side of the center line are very unlikely to arise from random variation alone (the 'rule of seven'), so they signal an assignable cause even though every point is within the limits. The sample 5 point was correctly investigated and fixed, but that does not make the later run go away. Something changed around sample 9 (a new ingredient batch, a worn nozzle, a shift change) and must be found before the line can be declared stable for handover.
how: On a control chart, act on any point beyond a control limit and on non-random patterns inside the limits (such as seven consecutive points on one side of the mean); investigate the cause rather than adjusting the process point by point.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Fixing the calibration explains sample 5 only; the seven-point run below the mean is a separate, unexplained signal of instability.
Incorrect — Control limits come from the process's own variation; widening them to hide a signal defeats the purpose of the chart.
Incorrect — Adjusting after every reading is tampering; it adds variation and does not find the cause of the downward shift.
Correct — Seven consecutive points below the mean indicate a non-random shift that must be investigated and resolved before handover.
deepDive: Control charts separate common-cause variation (inherent, random noise) from special or assignable causes (something specific changed). Typical signals are a point beyond a control limit, and a run of about seven consecutive points on one side of the mean, or trending in one direction. Control limits describe what the process does; specification limits describe what the customer requires, so a process can be in control yet incapable, or capable yet unstable. The book's quality guidance favors finding and removing causes early rather than relying on end-of-line inspection, which is why the run must be resolved before acceptance.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.3.1): cost of quality — conformance versus nonconformance costs
question: Last year, a firm that builds custom industrial control panels spent $40,000 on prevention (training and design reviews), $90,000 on appraisal (inspection and testing), $150,000 on internal failures (rework and scrap), and $220,000 on external failures (field repairs and warranty claims). For its next project the quality lead proposes adding $60,000 of prevention through design-for-assembly reviews and wiring fixtures. Pilot data suggests internal failure costs will fall by 40% and external failure costs by 50%, with appraisal unchanged. What is the projected total cost of quality?
hint: Recalculate each of the four categories separately, then add them back together.
why: Prevention becomes $40,000 + $60,000 = $100,000; appraisal stays at $90,000; internal failure falls 40% to $150,000 × 0.6 = $90,000; external failure falls 50% to $220,000 × 0.5 = $110,000. Total cost of quality = $100,000 + $90,000 + $90,000 + $110,000 = $390,000, down from $500,000. Spending $60,000 more on prevention saves $170,000 in failure costs, a net reduction of $110,000.
how: For cost-of-quality questions, update each category (prevention, appraisal, internal failure, external failure) on its own, then total them; investing in conformance usually pays off when it removes larger failure costs.
optionNotes: Correct — $100,000 prevention + $90,000 appraisal + $90,000 internal failure + $110,000 external failure = $390,000.
Incorrect — This applies the 40% reduction to external failures as well ($132,000), instead of the 50% reduction given for them.
Incorrect — This adds the prevention investment and the internal-failure saving but leaves external failures unchanged at $220,000.
Incorrect — This adds the $60,000 investment to last year's $500,000 total and ignores the projected drop in failure costs.
deepDive: The book groups prevention and appraisal as costs of conformance and internal and external failures as costs of nonconformance. External failures are usually the most expensive, because they add warranty costs, lost goodwill and sometimes legal exposure, so shifting money toward prevention tends to lower the total. The cost of change also rises the later a defect is found, which reinforces the case for preventing defects during design. On the exam, classify each cost carefully: training and design reviews are prevention, inspection and testing are appraisal, rework and scrap are internal failure, and warranty and recalls are external failure.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
topic: Deferring testing to a hardening sprint
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.3.2): cost of change — building quality into every increment
question: An agile team building a logistics tracking app is three sprints away from a planned release. To show more features at reviews, the developers propose removing automated regression testing from the definition of done for now and running all of that testing in a single 'hardening sprint' just before release. The product owner likes the idea because more stories would show as done. As the team's project manager, what is the BEST response?
options: Support the plan, since a hardening sprint is a common agile practice for catching defects just before a release
Accept the change, but ask a separate QA team to test each story in parallel so that defects surface a little sooner
Let the team decide on its own, because a self-organizing team owns its definition of done without outside input
Keep regression testing in the definition of done and help the product owner reduce the scope planned per sprint
hint: Think about when defects become most expensive to find, and what 'done' is supposed to tell stakeholders.
why: Moving testing out of the definition of done makes stories look finished when they are not, so reviews show false progress and defects pile up unseen until the hardening sprint, when they are costliest to fix and can threaten the release. Keeping regression testing in the definition of done preserves a genuinely releasable increment, and the honest lever is scope: the product owner can plan fewer stories per sprint so the team finishes them properly.
how: In agile delivery, protect the definition of done and adjust scope instead; deferring testing to the end recreates waterfall risk and hides the true state of the product.
optionNotes: Incorrect — A hardening sprint is usually a symptom of incomplete work, not a recommended practice; it delays feedback and hides defects.
Incorrect — A separate QA team still leaves stories reported as done before they are verified, and it creates hand-offs and delayed feedback.
Incorrect — The team does own its definition of done, but a servant leader should coach on the quality and transparency risks rather than stay silent.
Correct — It keeps each increment genuinely releasable and makes scope, not quality, the variable used to fit the sprint.
deepDive: The book's principle of building quality into processes and deliverables means catching defects close to where they are created, because the cost of change grows over time. In agile teams this shows up as a strong definition of done, automated tests and continuous integration, rather than end-phase testing. A 'hardening' or 'stabilization' sprint that collects deferred testing is a warning sign of undone work and technical debt. Exam items often tempt you with options that look productive (more stories done) but compromise transparency or quality.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
topic: Acceptance criteria for an AI model
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.2.1): requirements — measurable acceptance criteria for quality
question: An insurer's hybrid project is buying a machine-learning model from a vendor to triage incoming claims for fraud. The vendor reports 94% accuracy on its own test data. The claims director wants to sign the acceptance certificate so the model can go live next month, and the project's quality plan says only that the model must be 'accurate and fair.' About 6% of the insurer's claims are fraudulent, and the model will score claims from all regions. What should the project manager do before acceptance?
options: Accept the model, because 94% accuracy is above typical industry benchmarks and the vendor has warranted its results
Agree measurable criteria by claim type and region, then test the model on the insurer's own held-out claims data
Ask the vendor to retrain the model on more data until it reaches 99% accuracy on the vendor's own test set
Run the model live in shadow mode, and let the claims director judge later whether its outputs look fair enough
hint: With only 6% of claims fraudulent, how accurate would a model be if it never flagged any claim at all?
why: With 6% fraud, a model that labels every claim as legitimate would already score 94% accuracy, so the vendor's figure says nothing about whether fraud is being caught. 'Accurate and fair' is not verifiable either. Before acceptance, the project should agree measurable criteria (for example, the share of fraudulent claims detected and false-alarm rates, overall and by region and claim type) and test against the insurer's own held-out, representative data. Only then is an acceptance decision objective.
how: For any deliverable, and especially AI models, acceptance needs measurable, agreed criteria tested on representative independent data; a headline metric chosen by the supplier is not evidence of fitness for use.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Headline accuracy is misleading when fraud is rare, and a vendor warranty does not replace independent verification against agreed criteria.
Correct — Measurable criteria by segment, tested on the insurer's own held-out data, make acceptance objective and expose weak or unfair performance.
Incorrect — Chasing a higher score on the vendor's own data repeats the flaw; accuracy still hides missed fraud and uneven results by region.
Incorrect — Shadow running can be useful, but without agreed criteria the later judgment is subjective and fairness risks go unmeasured.
deepDive: Quality means meeting requirements and fitness for use, which requires requirements that are clear, measurable and testable. For classification models, accuracy is a weak measure when classes are imbalanced; precision, recall (detection rate), false-positive rates and performance across subgroups are more informative. Testing on the buyer's own held-out data guards against overfitting to the supplier's test set, and segment-level results reveal fairness issues. After go-live, monitoring for data drift keeps the model within the agreed quality thresholds.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.3): quality — prevention over inspection
question: A hybrid project is producing 2,000 smart-meter enclosures on a new assembly line while a software team builds the meter firmware in two-week sprints. Early units show two recurring defects: gaskets fitted upside down on the line, and firmware regressions that are found only during the monthly system test. The sponsor asks for changes that build quality in rather than catching defects afterwards. Which two actions BEST do this? (Select two.)
options: Add a fixture to the assembly station that physically prevents a gasket from being fitted upside down
Double the final inspection sample size for finished enclosures leaving the assembly line each day
Run automated regression tests on every firmware commit as part of the team's build pipeline
Add a second full system-test cycle for the firmware each month before every planned release
Pay inspectors a bonus for each defective enclosure they catch before it is shipped to the customer
hint: Which options stop a defect from being created or from surviving past the moment it appears?
why: A mistake-proofing fixture makes the gasket error physically impossible, and automated regression tests on every commit catch a firmware defect minutes after it is introduced. Both remove defects at their source instead of relying on later inspection. Larger inspection samples, extra system-test cycles and inspector bonuses all find defects after they have been created, which costs more and still lets some escape.
how: To build quality in, prevent the error (mistake-proofing, standard work) or detect it immediately where it happens (automated tests in the pipeline); extra end-of-line inspection is appraisal, not prevention.
optionNotes: Correct — Mistake-proofing (poka-yoke) prevents the defect from being made at all, which is the cheapest point to address quality.
Incorrect — A larger inspection sample is more appraisal; it may catch more bad units but does nothing to stop them being produced.
Correct — Testing every commit gives immediate feedback, so regressions are fixed when they are introduced rather than weeks later.
Incorrect — Another monthly test cycle still finds regressions long after they were created, keeping feedback slow and rework expensive.
Incorrect — Rewarding defect detection targets inspection, can distort behavior, and does not reduce the number of defects created.
deepDive: The book's quality ideas emphasize building quality into processes and deliverables so that defects are prevented or found close to their source. In manufacturing this means mistake-proofing, standard work and in-process checks; in software it means test automation, continuous integration and a robust definition of done. Both reduce the costs of nonconformance, especially external failure. On the exam, distinguish prevention and immediate detection from appraisal activities such as final inspection and extra test phases.

task: 7. Plan and optimize quality of products/deliverables
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 7 · Agile practice (definition of done versus acceptance criteria)
question: During preparation for the sprint review, a developer says a customer-profile story meets all of its acceptance criteria and the product owner has already tried it. However, the team's definition of done also requires a passed security scan and updated API documentation, and neither has been completed. The sprint ends tomorrow, and there is not enough time left to finish them. How should the team treat the story?
options: Treat it as not done: exclude it from this sprint's velocity and return the remaining work to the product backlog
Count half of its story points toward this sprint's velocity and finish the scan and documentation early in the next sprint
Mark it as done, and add a technical-debt item for the scan and documentation to the product backlog
Count it as done, because the product owner has seen it working and all of its acceptance criteria are met
hint: Acceptance criteria and the definition of done answer different questions — does this story need both?
why: Acceptance criteria describe what a specific story must do; the definition of done is the team-wide quality standard every item must meet. A story is done only when both are satisfied, so without the security scan and documentation it is not done. It is not shown as complete, earns no velocity, and returns to the product backlog for the product owner to reorder.
how: An item that does not meet the definition of done is not done, whatever its acceptance criteria say: no partial credit, no velocity, and the remaining work goes back to the product backlog.
optionNotes: Correct — Undone work is not presented as complete or counted in velocity; it returns to the product backlog to be reprioritized.
Incorrect — Agile teams do not take partial credit; counting half the points inflates velocity and distorts future forecasts.
Incorrect — Declaring it done while skipping required quality steps hides real work as technical debt and undermines transparency.
Incorrect — Meeting acceptance criteria is necessary but not sufficient; the definition of done still applies to every item.
deepDive: The definition of done is a shared quality commitment that makes an increment potentially releasable, while acceptance criteria are story-specific conditions set with the product owner. Security scans and documentation are typical definition-of-done items because they apply to all work. Counting partially finished work damages the reliability of velocity and release forecasts. Exam items often pair a satisfied product owner with an unmet definition of done to test whether you protect quality and transparency.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Planning Performance Domain (2.4.2.3): schedules — network logic, total float and free float
question: Refer to the exhibit. On a clinic fit-out project, the electrical subcontractor responsible for activity D asks to start D later than its early start date so that it can finish another job first. The crew for activity F is booked to start on F's early start date and cannot be moved without a penalty. How many days can activity D be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor activity?
options: 0 days
2 days
3 days
5 days
hint: The question protects the successor's start date, not just the project finish date — which kind of float does that describe?
why: Forward pass: A 0–3; B 3–17; C 3–7; D 7–9; E 7–12; F starts at the later of D and E, so F 12–15; G starts at the later of B and F, so G 17–21; H 21–24. The critical path is A-B-G-H (24 days). Free float of D = early start of F − early finish of D = 12 − 9 = 3 days. Total float of D is 5 days (late start 12 − early start 7), but using more than 3 days would push F's start and trigger the crew penalty.
how: Free float = earliest early start of the successors − early finish of the activity; total float = late start − early start. Use free float when a successor's start must not move, and total float when only the project finish date matters.
optionNotes: Incorrect — D is not on the critical path; it finishes on day 9 while F cannot start until E finishes on day 12.
Incorrect — Two days is the total float of the C-E-F path, not the slack between D's finish and F's early start.
Correct — F's early start (day 12) minus D's early finish (day 9) gives 3 days of free float.
Incorrect — Five days is D's total float; delays beyond 3 days would push F's start and trigger the crew penalty.
deepDive: Total float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project finish (or a constrained milestone); free float is how long it can slip without delaying any successor's early start. Free float is always less than or equal to total float, and an activity can have total float but no free float when it shares float with the rest of its path. Using float that belongs to a chain can make later activities critical, which is why schedulers watch near-critical paths. In practice, commitments like booked crews or delivery windows turn free float into the limit that matters.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Planning Performance Domain (2.4.2.2): estimating — probabilistic ranges and confidence
question: A laboratory relocation has three sequential critical-path activities with these three-point estimates in days (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic): decommissioning 8, 12, 22; moving and installation 15, 20, 31; requalification testing 4, 6, 14. The steering committee wants a duration range for this path that it can rely on with about 95% confidence. Using beta (PERT) estimates, what range should the project manager report?
options: 30 to 46 days
33 to 49 days
34 to 48 days
37 to 45 days
hint: Standard deviations do not add along a path, but something else about them does.
why: PERT means: (8 + 4×12 + 22)/6 = 13; (15 + 4×20 + 31)/6 = 21; (4 + 4×6 + 14)/6 = 7; path mean = 41 days. Standard deviations (P − O)/6: 2.33, 2.67 and 1.67; variances 5.44 + 7.11 + 2.78 = 15.33; path standard deviation = √15.33 ≈ 3.9 days. About 95% confidence is ±2σ: 41 ± 7.8 ≈ 33 to 49 days.
how: For a path estimate, add the PERT means, add the variances (σ²), then take the square root to get the path σ; ±1σ ≈ 68%, ±2σ ≈ 95%, ±3σ ≈ 99.7%.
optionNotes: Incorrect — This centers the range on the most-likely total (38 days) instead of the PERT mean of 41 days.
Correct — The mean is 41 days and the path σ is √15.33 ≈ 3.9, so ±2σ gives roughly 33 to 49 days.
Incorrect — This adds the three standard deviations (6.7 days) and applies them once; σ values must be combined through their variances.
Incorrect — This is only ±1σ around 41 days, which gives about 68% confidence rather than the 95% the committee asked for.
deepDive: Three-point estimating turns uncertainty into a range: the beta (PERT) mean weights the most-likely value four times, while the triangular mean is a simple average. The book contrasts deterministic single-point estimates with probabilistic ones that express confidence levels, which is what a steering committee needs for commitments. Because independent uncertainties partly offset each other, the path standard deviation is smaller than the sum of the individual deviations. For whole-network risk with merging paths, Monte Carlo simulation gives a better picture than a single-path calculation.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.2.7): forecasts — throughput and scope trends
question: A product team building a field-inspection app has 210 story points remaining in its release backlog. Over the last five sprints its velocity averaged 32 points (ranging from 28 to 36), while the product owner added an average of 11 points of new stories each sprint in response to user feedback, and she expects that pattern to continue. The sponsor asks how many more sprints the release will take if both average trends hold. What should the project manager forecast?
options: About 5 sprints
About 7 sprints
About 10 sprints
About 13 sprints
hint: If new work keeps arriving while the team burns work down, what is the real rate at which the remaining backlog shrinks?
why: The backlog shrinks by velocity minus scope growth: 32 − 11 = 21 points per sprint. Sprints needed = 210 ÷ 21 = 10. Ignoring growth (210 ÷ 32 ≈ 6.6) would promise about 7 sprints and create a false expectation; the project manager should also show the product owner and sponsor that trimming new additions is the lever that pulls the date in.
how: When scope keeps growing, forecast with the net burn rate (velocity − average scope added per sprint) and make the scope trend visible, for example on a burnup chart.
optionNotes: Incorrect — This adds scope growth to velocity (210 ÷ 43 ≈ 4.9); new work slows net progress, it does not speed it up.
Incorrect — This divides by velocity alone (210 ÷ 32 ≈ 6.6) and ignores the 11 points of new scope arriving every sprint.
Correct — Net burn is 32 − 11 = 21 points per sprint, so 210 ÷ 21 = 10 sprints if both trends hold.
Incorrect — This uses the lowest velocity (210 ÷ 17 ≈ 12.4), a pessimistic bound rather than the average-trend forecast requested.
deepDive: Burnup charts show two lines, total scope and completed work, so both velocity and scope change are visible; burndown charts can hide scope growth. Forecasts based on throughput become more reliable as data accumulates, and good practice presents a range (for example, using the best and worst sprints) alongside the average-based estimate. The book treats forecasts as a key measurement output that lets stakeholders make decisions, here whether to cap new scope or accept a later release. On the exam, watch for options that silently ignore scope growth or rely on the single best sprint.

topic: Forecasting one item with cycle time
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 8 · Flow-based (Kanban) forecasting with cycle-time percentiles
question: A support-tools team uses Kanban with no sprints or estimates. A regional director asks when a newly requested report-export feature will be finished; the item was pulled into 'In progress' this morning. Over the last three months, the team's cycle-time data shows that 50% of similar items finished within 4 days and 85% within 9 days, with a few outliers near 20 days. What is the MOST appropriate answer to give the director?
options: It will be done in 4 days, the median cycle time, because half of all similar items have finished that quickly
It will be done within 20 days, because quoting the slowest outlier guarantees that the date will not be missed
No date can be given until the work is broken into tasks and every task has been estimated in hours
There is about an 85% chance it will be done within 9 days, based on the team's recent cycle-time history
hint: What does the team's own history say about how likely different finish dates are?
why: Flow teams forecast single items from their cycle-time distribution. Quoting the 85th percentile gives the director a date with a stated, fairly high likelihood, and it is based on real performance rather than guesses. The median would be missed about half the time, the worst outlier pads the date so much that it misleads, and demanding hour estimates adds effort without improving on the team's actual data.
how: In Kanban, answer 'when will it be done?' with a probabilistic forecast from historical cycle time (for example, the 85th percentile), and keep refreshing it as data accumulates.
optionNotes: Incorrect — The median is a coin flip: about half of similar items took longer, so this date would often be missed.
Incorrect — Quoting the extreme outlier overstates the likely time and makes the team's delivery look far slower than it really is.
Incorrect — Detailed hour estimates are unnecessary when stable historical flow data already gives a reliable probabilistic forecast.
Correct — A percentile-based forecast gives a realistic date with an explicit confidence level drawn from the team's actual history.
deepDive: Cycle time is the time from when work starts on an item until it is finished; lead time runs from request to delivery. Many flow teams publish a service level expectation such as '85% of items finish within 9 days' and use scatter plots or cycle-time charts to track it. Keeping work in progress low makes cycle times shorter and more predictable, per Little's Law. On the exam, prefer answers that give ranges or probabilities based on empirical data over single-point promises.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Uncertainty Performance Domain (2.8.5.3): visible schedule reserve instead of padded estimates
question: A hybrid project is fitting out a new data center for an insurer: the building work follows a detailed schedule, while agile teams migrate applications in sprints. Reviewing the fit-out schedule, the project manager learns that each work-package owner quietly added 20–30% 'safety' to every activity estimate. Even so, almost no activity finishes early: most start late and end on or after their padded dates, and the fit-out is now three weeks behind at its midpoint. What should the project manager do?
options: Agree realistic estimates with owners and move the removed safety into a visible schedule reserve the project tracks
Ask the owners to add a larger safety margin to the remaining estimates, since the current padding has proven too small
Crash the remaining critical activities with overtime and extra crews so that the three lost weeks are recovered quickly
Keep the current estimates but move from monthly to weekly progress reports so that late starts become visible sooner
hint: If generous estimates still produce late finishes, where is the safety actually going?
why: Hidden padding tends to be consumed rather than saved: people start later because the estimate feels roomy (student syndrome) and work expands to fill the time available (Parkinson's law), so delays pass down the chain while early finishes almost never do. Replacing padded durations with realistic estimates and holding the removed safety as an explicit, shared schedule reserve lets the project manager see how fast reserve is being used and act on it, usually with a smaller total than the sum of the individual pads. More padding repeats the cause, crashing buys back time at extra cost without fixing it, and more frequent reporting only watches the same behavior more closely.
how: Keep activity estimates realistic and hold schedule contingency as a visible reserve owned and tracked at project level, such as a project buffer; padding hidden inside each estimate is usually consumed and gives no early warning.
optionNotes: Correct — Realistic estimates plus a visible, shared reserve remove the incentive to use up padding and show clearly how fast contingency is consumed.
Incorrect — More padding feeds the same late-start behavior, lengthens the plan further, and makes the schedule even less honest.
Incorrect — Crashing may recover time at added cost, but the hidden padding and late starts would keep eroding the rest of the schedule.
Incorrect — More frequent reporting improves visibility a little but leaves the padded estimates and late-start habits, the real cause, untouched.
deepDive: PMBOK 7 treats reserve as an explicit amount of time or budget set aside for uncertainty, sized by reserve analysis and monitored against the remaining risk. Critical chain scheduling applies the same idea: it removes safety from individual activities, aggregates part of it into a project buffer at the end of the chain (with feeding buffers where paths merge), and manages the project by buffer consumption. Because variation pools, a shared buffer can be smaller than the sum of individual pads. Exam traps include 'add more contingency to each activity' and treating crashing as the answer to every delay.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.2.3 and 2.7.5): earned value and variance thresholds
question: Refer to the exhibit. On a water-treatment plant upgrade, the cost management plan requires a variance analysis and an exception plan for any control account whose CPI or SPI falls below 0.90. The monthly report prepared by a planner shows the project as 'green' because the overall CPI and SPI are both above 0.90. Which control accounts require an exception plan this month?
options: None, because the project's overall CPI and SPI are both still above the 0.90 threshold
Electrical only, because its schedule variance is the largest of the four in dollar terms
Controls only, because its cost overrun is the largest of the four accounts in dollar terms
Electrical and Controls, because each has one index below the 0.90 threshold this month
hint: The threshold applies at the level the plan specifies; check both indices for every account.
why: Electrical: SPI = 255 ÷ 300 = 0.85 and CPI = 255 ÷ 270 = 0.94. Controls: CPI = 190 ÷ 225 = 0.84 and SPI = 190 ÷ 200 = 0.95. Civil works (CPI 1.02, SPI 1.05) and Commissioning (0.95, 0.95) are within threshold. The totals (CPI = 960 ÷ 1,005 = 0.96, SPI = 960 ÷ 1,000 = 0.96) look healthy only because Civil works' good performance offsets the problems, so both Electrical and Controls need exception plans.
how: Evaluate earned value at the level where the thresholds are set (usually the control account); aggregate indices can hide serious local variances.
optionNotes: Incorrect — The plan sets thresholds per control account; good project-level totals mask two accounts that breach the limit.
Incorrect — Electrical does breach on SPI (0.85), but Controls also breaches on CPI (0.84), so it cannot be the only one.
Incorrect — Controls breaches on CPI (0.84), but Electrical's SPI of 0.85 is also below the threshold and needs a plan.
Correct — Electrical's SPI (0.85) and Controls' CPI (0.84) are each below 0.90, so both require an exception plan.
deepDive: CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV; values below 1.0 mean over budget or behind schedule. The book notes that thresholds reflect stakeholder risk tolerance and that an exception plan can be as simple as a meeting to agree actions, followed by checks that the plan is working. It also encourages acting before a breach when a trend forecasts one. Rolling everything up into a single project-level status is a common way that 'green' reports hide trouble, so good dashboards let viewers drill into control accounts.
