source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.3): presenting information — burndown charts
question: Refer to the exhibit. A team building an e-commerce checkout has produced burndown charts with this same shape for its last three sprints. Each time, most stories were accepted in the final two days and one or two were carried over. The developers say the chart is 'just cosmetic' because they nearly finish the sprint anyway. What should the project manager suggest in the retrospective?
options: Re-estimate the work in task hours instead of story points, so that the remaining-work line drops each day
Slice stories smaller and limit work in progress, so that stories are finished and accepted throughout the sprint
Plan far fewer stories into each sprint, since the chart shows the team is committing to much more than it can finish
Keep the current approach, since nearly all stories get finished and the burndown is only a reporting artifact
hint: What has to be true about the work for points to burn down only in the last two days?
why: Story points burn down only when stories are done, so a flat line followed by a cliff means many stories are in progress at once and finish (or get tested and accepted) only at the end. That delays feedback, hides risk until it is too late to react, and causes the repeated carryover. Smaller stories and a work-in-progress limit let the team finish items continuously, which makes the chart meaningful and the sprint more predictable.
how: A burndown that stays flat and then drops sharply signals large stories or too much work in progress; fix the flow (smaller slices, WIP limits, test as you go) rather than the chart.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Burning down task hours changes the picture, not the problem; stories would still finish late and carry over.
Correct — Smaller stories and WIP limits create a steady flow of finished work and earlier feedback within each sprint.
Incorrect — The team nearly finishes each sprint, so capacity is not the main issue; late completion comes from how the work flows.
Incorrect — Repeated carryover and late feedback are real risks; the chart is showing a genuine delivery problem, not a cosmetic one.
deepDive: Burndown charts are information radiators that show remaining work against an ideal line; their value lies in the conversations they prompt. Common patterns include a flat line (blocked work), a rising line (scope added), and a late cliff ('hockey stick') from large or batched work. The remedies come from flow thinking: slice vertically, swarm on the top item, limit WIP, and integrate and test continuously. The book stresses that measures exist to support learning and improvement, not to be dismissed or gamed.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.2.2): delivery — flow, work in progress and bottlenecks
question: Refer to the exhibit. A seven-developer payments platform team requires every change to pass a security code review, and only one senior engineer is currently qualified to perform it. Stakeholders complain that finished features take longer and longer to reach production, yet the developers report being fully busy and are starting new items every week. What should the project manager do?
options: Encourage the developers to start more new items each week, so that plenty of work is ready once reviews speed up
Ask the sponsor to approve skipping the security review for low-risk changes until the review queue has been cleared
Facilitate a WIP limit on review and have developers pair with the senior engineer to clear and share the reviews
Request two more developers for the team, so that it can increase its output and deliver more features each week
hint: Adding work upstream of a constraint rarely helps — where does the diagram show work piling up?
why: The 'In review' band widens every week while the 'Done' band flattens, so review is the bottleneck: work arrives faster than it leaves, and lead time keeps growing. Starting more items or adding developers only feeds the queue. A WIP limit on review stops new starts once the queue is full, and developers pairing with the senior engineer both clears the backlog and grows review capacity, without dropping a required security control.
how: When a CFD band widens, that stage is the constraint: stop starting and start finishing, set WIP limits, swarm on the bottleneck, and build capacity there rather than upstream.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Starting more work increases WIP in front of the bottleneck, which lengthens lead times further (Little's Law).
Incorrect — Dropping a required security control to speed flow trades a delivery problem for a compliance and security risk.
Correct — A WIP limit exposes and contains the queue, and pairing clears reviews while cross-training more reviewers.
Incorrect — More developers raise the arrival rate at review; throughput is capped by the single reviewer, so the queue grows faster.
deepDive: A cumulative flow diagram shows how many items sit in each state over time. Parallel bands mean stable flow; a widening band marks a bottleneck; a flattening 'Done' band means throughput is falling; the horizontal distance between bands approximates lead time. The book lists flow measures such as WIP, cycle time and throughput as key delivery metrics. The theory of constraints adds that improving anything other than the bottleneck does not raise system throughput.

exhibit.title: Cumulative flow diagram — payments platform team

topic: Why status stays green until red
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.4 and 2.7.5): measurement pitfalls and threshold-based exception plans
question: In a hybrid ERP program, any workstream that reports amber must present a recovery plan at the monthly executive review, which leads describe as 'a public grilling.' For the third time this year, a workstream reported green for months and then jumped straight to red two weeks before a milestone. The sponsor asks the project manager to stop these surprises. What should the project manager do?
options: Require each workstream lead to sign a formal statement confirming that the weekly status they report is accurate
Add an independent monthly audit of every workstream, so that inaccurate green reports are exposed and penalized
Replace the red-amber-green ratings with detailed written narratives, so that executives can read the full context each month
Base status on agreed objective thresholds and forecasts, and work with the sponsor to treat amber as a call for help
hint: Ask why capable leads would keep reporting green when they can see problems coming.
why: The pattern points to a system problem: amber brings public criticism, so leads avoid it until a problem can no longer be hidden. Anchoring status in objective, agreed thresholds and forward-looking forecasts removes much of the subjectivity, and changing how the executive review responds to amber (support rather than blame) makes early warning safe. Signed statements and punitive audits deepen the fear, and narratives without objective criteria still allow optimism to hide trends.
how: When status reports stay green until they suddenly turn red, fix both the measure (objective thresholds, forecasts) and the incentive (make bad news safe to report early).
optionNotes: Incorrect — A signed declaration adds pressure without changing the incentive to hide problems, so status stays green until it can't.
Incorrect — Punitive audits increase fear and defensiveness; they may catch late problems but will not encourage early warnings.
Incorrect — Narratives add context, but without objective criteria and a safer response to bad news, optimistic reporting continues.
Correct — Objective thresholds and forecasts reduce subjectivity, and treating amber as a request for support makes early warnings safe.
deepDive: 'Watermelon' reporting (green outside, red inside) usually grows from incentives: when bad news is punished, people delay reporting it. The book's measurement pitfalls include misuse of metrics and confirmation bias, and it recommends thresholds with agreed exception plans, ideally acting when a breach is forecast rather than after it happens. Leading indicators and trend-based forecasts give earlier signals than milestone status. Leaders build psychological safety by responding to amber with help, which turns reporting into an early-warning system.

topic: Replacing vanity metrics on a dashboard
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.4): measurement pitfalls — vanity metrics
question: A product team is rebuilding a university's course-registration website. Its dashboard, displayed as an information radiator in the team room and emailed weekly to the sponsor, shows total page views, story points completed, and lines of code written, all rising steadily. The sponsor says, 'The numbers look great, but I still can't tell whether students are finding it easier to register.' What should the project manager do?
options: Work with the product owner to add outcome measures, such as registration completion rate and time to register
Add more detail to the current charts, such as page views by browser type and story points by individual developer
Explain to the sponsor that rising output metrics are reliable evidence that the desired outcomes will follow later
Stop sending the dashboard to the sponsor, and provide a weekly narrative status report written by the team instead
hint: Which kind of measure would actually answer the sponsor's question?
why: Page views, story points and lines of code show activity but do not help anyone decide whether students are better served; they are vanity metrics. The sponsor's question concerns an outcome, so the dashboard should track measures such as registration completion rate, time to register, and help-desk calls about registration, agreed with the product owner who owns value. Output metrics can remain for the team's own use, but they should not stand in for outcomes.
how: Choose metrics that inform decisions about value and outcomes; drop or demote vanity metrics that only show activity or volume.
optionNotes: Correct — Outcome measures tied to the sponsor's goal show whether the product is delivering value to students.
Incorrect — Slicing vanity metrics more finely adds noise, and per-developer points invite gaming without answering the question.
Incorrect — Output does not guarantee outcomes; a team can deliver many features that do not make registration easier.
Incorrect — Withdrawing the dashboard reduces transparency; the problem is what it measures, not the fact that it is shared.
deepDive: A vanity metric shows data that looks impressive but does not help make decisions — the book contrasts page views with measures such as new users. Useful measures are tied to objectives, specific and actionable, and they include business value and stakeholder outcomes, not just delivery output. Dashboards and information radiators should highlight the few measures that matter, with detail available on demand. On the exam, prefer answers that shift reporting from outputs to outcomes.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.4): measurement pitfalls — the Hawthorne effect
question: During a system-replacement project, a service desk manager began publishing a weekly leaderboard of tickets closed per analyst to show that the new tool was improving performance. Within a month, tickets closed rose 30%, but reopened tickets doubled and customer satisfaction scores fell. Analysts admit they now close tickets quickly and split complex issues into several smaller tickets. The manager asks the project manager how to fix the measurement. What is the BEST recommendation?
options: Keep the leaderboard, but add a penalty for any analyst whose reopened tickets exceed an agreed weekly limit
Stop publishing any service desk metrics, so that analysts can focus on their work without pressure to perform
Measure outcomes at team level, such as first-contact resolution and satisfaction, and review them with the analysts
Keep the leaderboard for another quarter, since the drop in quality is probably a short-lived adjustment period
hint: The act of measuring changed what people did — so what should be measured, and at what level, to encourage the behavior you actually want?
why: Publishing individual closure counts changed behavior toward the number itself: analysts optimized for volume, splitting tickets and closing them prematurely, at the expense of customers. Replacing it with team-level outcome measures (first-contact resolution, reopen rate, satisfaction) aligns the metric with the real goal, and reviewing results with the analysts builds ownership rather than pressure. Penalties add another number to game, dropping all metrics removes useful feedback, and waiting ignores clear evidence of harm.
how: Because measuring something changes behavior, choose balanced outcome measures that reward the result you want, prefer team-level metrics, and watch for gaming.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Adding a penalty keeps the harmful incentive and invites new gaming, such as avoiding reopening tickets that are not truly resolved.
Incorrect — Removing all metrics throws away useful feedback; the problem is the choice of measure, not measurement itself.
Correct — Team-level outcome measures align behavior with customer results, and reviewing them with the analysts builds ownership.
Incorrect — The data already shows real harm to customers; waiting another quarter lets the damage and the gaming habits grow.
deepDive: The Hawthorne effect is the observation that the act of measuring influences behavior; the book warns that measuring only output can push teams toward volume rather than customer value. Related pitfalls include misusing metrics (optimizing short-term numbers at the expense of long-term outcomes) and demoralization from unachievable targets. Balanced measures, pairing quantity with quality and outcome metrics, reduce gaming. Individual leaderboards also damage collaboration, which is why agile and lean practices favor team-level measures.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.1.1): key performance indicators — leading and lagging
question: A hybrid project is rolling out a new electronic health record module across 12 clinics over six months, with software configured in sprints and clinic go-lives on a fixed schedule. The sponsor's dashboard currently shows only cost variance and milestones achieved, both reported at month end. She wants measures that will warn her early if clinic adoption, the main expected benefit, is at risk. Which two measures would BEST serve as leading indicators? (Select two.)
options: Percentage of clinic staff who have completed hands-on training before their clinic's go-live date
Total project cost variance at the end of each month compared with the approved cost baseline
Number of milestones completed to date compared with the approved schedule baseline
Trend in unresolved workflow issues raised by clinics that are preparing to go live
Final adoption rate across all clinics, measured six months after the last go-live
hint: Look for measures that change before adoption does, and that are connected to what drives it.
why: Training completion before go-live and the trend in unresolved workflow issues both move ahead of adoption and are causally linked to it: untrained staff and unresolved workflow problems are the usual reasons clinicians avoid a new system. They give the sponsor time to act. Cost variance and milestones are lagging measures of project performance that say little about adoption, and the final adoption rate is the lagging outcome itself, available only after it is too late to intervene.
how: Leading indicators predict future results and allow timely action; lagging indicators confirm what has already happened. Pair a lagging outcome with a few leading drivers you can still influence.
optionNotes: Correct — Readiness through training is a predictor of adoption and can be acted on clinic by clinic before each go-live.
Incorrect — Cost variance is a lagging measure of spending performance and does not signal whether clinics will adopt the system.
Incorrect — Milestones achieved show past schedule performance; a milestone can be met even while adoption risk is growing.
Correct — A rising count of unresolved workflow issues warns that clinicians may resist or work around the system after go-live.
Incorrect — This is the lagging outcome itself; it arrives months after the project has ended, too late to change anything.
deepDive: The book describes leading indicators as predicting changes or trends, and lagging indicators as measuring deliverables or events after the fact. Lagging measures are easier to collect, which is why dashboards often default to them, but they leave no time to respond. Good benefit tracking pairs the lagging outcome (adoption rate) with leading drivers such as readiness, training, and issue trends. For change-heavy rollouts, change-readiness assessments and early usage in pilot clinics are further useful leading signals.

topic: EAC with cost and schedule pressure
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Measurement Performance Domain (2.7.2.7): forecasts — estimate at completion variants
question: A fixed-date data-center migration has a budget at completion of $2,400,000. At the latest status date, planned value is $1,200,000, earned value is $1,000,000, and actual cost is $1,250,000. The contract completion date cannot move, so the remaining work will need paid overtime and extra contractors to recover the schedule, and the team agrees that both cost and schedule performance will influence the remaining costs. What is the most appropriate estimate at completion?
hint: Pick the EAC formula that matches the stated assumption about what will drive the remaining work's cost.
why: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 1,000,000 ÷ 1,250,000 = 0.80; SPI = EV ÷ PV = 1,000,000 ÷ 1,200,000 ≈ 0.833; CPI × SPI ≈ 0.667. Because both indices are expected to affect the remaining work, EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI) = 1,250,000 + 1,400,000 ÷ 0.667 = 1,250,000 + 2,100,000 = $3,350,000. That implies a variance at completion of about −$950,000, which should go to the sponsor with recovery options.
how: Choose the EAC by assumption: atypical variance → AC + (BAC − EV); current cost performance continues → BAC ÷ CPI; both cost and schedule pressure continue → AC + (BAC − EV) ÷ (CPI × SPI).
optionNotes: Incorrect — AC + (BAC − EV) assumes the overrun was a one-off and the rest runs to budget, which contradicts the overtime assumption.
Incorrect — BAC ÷ SPI is not a recognized EAC formula; it wrongly uses schedule performance on its own to scale costs.
Incorrect — BAC ÷ CPI assumes only current cost performance continues and ignores the extra cost of recovering the schedule.
deepDive: Forecasting is one of the book's key measurement outputs: EAC, ETC, VAC and TCPI turn past performance into a view of the future that stakeholders can act on. The composite CPI × SPI formula is used when a firm deadline forces the team to buy back schedule, so poor schedule performance also inflates future costs. ETC here is $2,100,000, and the TCPI needed to finish within BAC would be (2,400,000 − 1,000,000) ÷ (2,400,000 − 1,250,000) ≈ 1.22, an unrealistic jump from 0.80. On the exam, read the stem's assumption carefully; it decides which formula applies.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Development Approach and Life Cycle Performance Domain (2.3): deploy and close — transition for sustainment
question: A hybrid project replaced a distribution company's warehouse management system four weeks ago. The transition plan, signed by the operations director, says the project closes when the in-house support team resolves priority-2 incidents without project help for two consecutive weeks. Support is still escalating about 60% of those incidents to the project's developers, who are due to join another project on Friday, the day the sponsor wants the project closed. What should the project manager do FIRST?
options: Close the project on Friday as planned and give the support team the developers' contact details for follow-up questions
Review the gap against the transition criteria with the operations director and sponsor, and agree how to close it
Keep the developers on the project until escalations stop, and inform the other project that their start is delayed
Declare the transition complete, because the operations director signed the go-live acceptance four weeks ago
hint: The exit condition for this project was agreed in writing — who agreed it, and has it been met?
why: The signed transition plan makes independent support of priority-2 incidents an exit criterion, and it has not been met. Before anything else, the project manager should make the gap visible to the operations director and sponsor and agree a response, such as targeted knowledge transfer, a short extension approved through change control, or a documented, accepted handover of the remaining risk. Closing anyway or declaring success breaks the agreement, and unilaterally holding the developers ignores the sponsor and the other project.
how: Closure depends on the agreed transition or acceptance criteria; when they are not met, surface the gap to the accountable stakeholders and agree a plan rather than closing by the calendar or acting alone.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Closing with unmet transition criteria leaves operations dependent on people who are gone, and breaks the signed plan.
Correct — The agreed criteria are unmet, so the accountable stakeholders need to see the gap and agree how it will be closed.
Incorrect — Holding the developers indefinitely is a unilateral decision that affects another project and the sponsor's plans.
Incorrect — Go-live acceptance is not the same as transition acceptance; the signed plan sets a separate operational readiness test.
deepDive: The book's life cycle view ends deployment only when the transition activities needed for sustainment, benefits realization and organizational change are complete. Transition or hypercare exit criteria (incident volumes, independent support, runbooks, training) define when operations can own the product. When they are not met, options include extending hypercare, focused coaching, or a formal risk acceptance by the receiving owner, each decided by the accountable stakeholders. Exam traps include closing on the planned date regardless, or confusing go-live acceptance with operational handover.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Stewardship principle: financial integrity and returning unused funds at closure
question: A project to upgrade the network in a city's 12 public libraries has been accepted and is two weeks from closure. It will finish about $38,000 under budget, including $25,000 of contingency reserve that was never needed. The technical lead suggests spending the remainder on spare laptops and new meeting-room screens before the books close, warning that 'unspent money gets clawed back and next year's budget will be cut.' The sponsor has not yet been told about the underspend. What should the project manager do?
options: Report the underspend to the sponsor, release the unused funds at closure, and route extras through normal funding
Buy the laptops and screens before closure, because they serve the same library users the project was set up to help
Keep the unused funds in the project account after closure so that they can cover any network problems found later
Move the unused funds to another project the team runs that is currently forecast to finish slightly over its budget
hint: Whose money is the underspend, and who decides how it should be used?
why: The funds were authorized for the approved scope, which is now delivered, and the unused contingency existed only for risks that did not occur. Stewardship and honesty require the project manager to report the underspend to the sponsor and return what is left through financial closure; if the laptops and screens are worthwhile, they should compete for funding through the normal process. Spending the money on extras is unapproved scope and gold plating, keeping a pot open after closure defeats financial control, and moving funds to another project is a decision the project manager has no authority to make.
how: At closure, report under- and overspends transparently, release unused funds and reserves to the organization, and send any new ideas through the normal funding or change process instead of spending leftover budget.
optionNotes: Correct — Transparent reporting and returning unused funds honor the approval that was given, and good ideas can still be funded through the normal route.
Incorrect — Spending leftover budget on items outside the approved scope is gold plating and uses funds without the sponsor's authorization.
Incorrect — Keeping money in a closed project's account undermines financial control; post-closure support belongs to operations and its own budget.
Incorrect — Reallocating funds between projects is a governance decision, and doing it quietly hides both projects' true financial performance.
deepDive: PMBOK 7 describes stewardship as acting with integrity, care and trustworthiness in using what the organization entrusts to a project, including its money. Contingency reserve covers identified risks and management reserve covers unknowns; neither becomes free budget when the risks do not occur. Financial closure reconciles actual costs, closes accounts and purchase orders, and returns what is unspent, while the final report explains variances in either direction. 'Use it or lose it' spending is a common organizational habit, but on the exam the honest, transparent path wins, and a recurring underspend is a useful estimating lesson.

topic: Final payment with open punch-list items
source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Project Work Performance Domain (2.5.6): working with procurements — closing the contract
question: A contractor has finished building a new operations center for a regional utility. The certificate of occupancy has been issued, but 11 minor punch-list items remain open, such as damaged ceiling tiles and a door closer that does not latch. The contractor has submitted its final invoice, including the 5% retainage that the contract allows the utility to hold until all punch-list items are complete. The utility's finance team wants to pay everything so the contract can be closed this month. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Pay the full invoice, including retainage, because the certificate of occupancy shows that the building is complete
Pay the full invoice now, and deduct the cost of the open punch-list items from a future contract with the contractor
Pay the invoice less the retainage, agree a date to finish the punch list, and close the contract once it is verified
Refuse the whole invoice until every punch-list item is fixed, to keep maximum pressure on the contractor to finish
hint: What does the contract itself say about when the held-back money is released?
why: Retainage exists exactly for this situation: the contract lets the utility withhold 5% until the punch list is complete. Paying the undisputed balance honors the contract, while holding the retainage keeps an incentive to finish. Agreeing a completion date and verifying the work before final payment and formal contract closure keeps the process fair and documented. Paying in full removes the leverage, and refusing the whole invoice would breach the payment terms.
how: Close contracts according to their terms: verify that all deliverables are complete and accepted, release holdbacks only when their conditions are met, settle open items or claims, then issue formal written closure.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Occupancy shows the building can be used, not that every contract obligation is complete; retainage conditions are still unmet.
Incorrect — Offsetting against a future, separate contract is informal, may not be enforceable, and leaves this contract's obligations unresolved.
Correct — It follows the contract: pay what is due, hold retainage until the punch list is verified, then close formally.
Incorrect — Withholding the undisputed amount breaches the payment terms and invites a claim, harming the relationship unnecessarily.
deepDive: Procurement closure typically includes confirming that all work and deliverables are accepted, resolving open claims or disputes, making final payments (including releasing retainage), updating supplier performance records and archiving the contract file. Retainage is a common construction mechanism that protects the buyer until final completion. The book notes that contracts define obligations for both parties, so the buyer must also meet its payment obligations. Exam items often test whether you follow the contract terms rather than informal shortcuts.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Project Work Performance Domain (2.5.8.2): explicit and tacit knowledge
question: A hybrid project to modernize a bank's payment interfaces is in its final month. The contract of the lead integration engineer, a contractor, ends in two weeks. She is the only person who understands several undocumented workarounds in the deployment process, and the operations engineers who will support the system have so far only read her short written notes. What is the BEST way for the project manager to prepare for her release?
options: Ask her to write a complete deployment manual in her final two weeks and store it in the knowledge repository
Arrange paired deployments and walkthroughs with the operations engineers, and record the key points that come up
Extend her contract by six months, so that she remains available to support the operations engineers after closure
Record a video of her explaining the deployment process and share it with the operations team before she leaves
hint: Some knowledge lives in experience rather than in documents — how is that kind usually passed on?
why: Workarounds learned through experience are tacit knowledge, which is hard to write down and is best shared by connecting people, for example through pairing, shadowing and hands-on walkthroughs. Having the operations engineers perform real deployments alongside her in the last two weeks transfers that know-how, and recording the key points they uncover turns part of it into explicit knowledge for the future. A manual or video alone captures only what she thinks to explain, and a six-month extension is costly and only postpones the transfer.
how: Codify explicit knowledge in documents and repositories, but transfer tacit knowledge through interaction: pairing, shadowing, mentoring, and hands-on practice before people are released.
optionNotes: Incorrect — A manual captures only explicit knowledge, and two weeks of writing leaves no time for the engineers to practice.
Correct — Pairing and walkthroughs transfer tacit know-how through practice, and recording what emerges adds useful explicit knowledge.
Incorrect — A long extension adds cost and delays closure while leaving the dependency on one person in place.
Incorrect — A video is one-way; it misses the judgment calls that surface only when engineers perform the deployment themselves.
deepDive: The book distinguishes explicit knowledge, which can be codified in words, pictures or numbers, from tacit knowledge, such as experience, insight and practical skill, which is shared by connecting people through conversation, mentoring and working together. Releasing resources at closure is a key moment for knowledge loss, especially with contractors. Good release planning combines documentation with structured hand-offs, so the receiving team can operate independently. On the exam, prefer answers that transfer knowledge through interaction when the knowledge is experiential.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Project Work Performance Domain (2.5.8): learning throughout the project — knowledge management
question: At the close of a laboratory construction project, the team's lessons-learned review found that long-lead equipment was ordered late, just as on the organization's previous two lab projects, because the procurement checklist does not flag items with lead times over 20 weeks. The PMO's repository already contains similar lessons from those earlier projects. What should the project manager do to make this lesson most useful to future projects?
options: Add this lesson to the repository with a high-priority tag, so that future project managers are more likely to find it
Present the lesson at the project's closing celebration, so that the whole team remembers it on its next assignment
Email the lesson to every project manager, and ask them all to review the repository before they start planning
Work with the PMO and procurement to update the checklist so that long-lead items are flagged during planning
hint: The same lesson has already been recorded twice — what would stop it from being recorded a fourth time?
why: The lesson has been captured on three projects but never acted on, so it has been identified, not learned. The most useful step is to change the organizational process asset that causes the problem, updating the procurement checklist with the PMO and procurement so long-lead items are flagged automatically. Future teams then benefit without having to find and read a lesson. Tagging, presenting or emailing the lesson repeats the approach that has already failed twice.
how: A lesson is learned only when it changes how work is done: turn recurring lessons into updated templates, checklists, standards or estimating data owned by the right function.
optionNotes: Incorrect — The repository already holds this lesson from two projects; better tagging still relies on someone finding and applying it.
Incorrect — Sharing it with this team helps a few people remember, but it does not change the process that caused the problem.
Incorrect — Mass email adds noise and depends on individual follow-through, which has not worked on the previous projects.
Correct — Updating the checklist builds the lesson into the organization's process, so every future project benefits automatically.
deepDive: The book treats learning as continuous: teams capture explicit knowledge in lessons learned and repositories, and tacit knowledge through conversation and mentoring. But repositories are only valuable when knowledge is applied; recurring issues are a sign that lessons are being recorded, not learned. Updating organizational process assets such as checklists, templates and estimating guides embeds the change. PMOs often own this step, linking project lessons to improvements in methods and tools.

source: Book: PMBOK Guide 7th ed. (PMI, 2021) — Delivery Performance Domain (2.6.4): suboptimal outcomes and deliberate investment in uncertainty
question: An innovation team inside an insurance company has spent four sprints testing whether small-business owners will buy cyber insurance through a chatbot. Every experiment agreed with the sponsor at the outset has missed its success threshold, including a pilot in which only 3 of 400 invited owners completed a purchase. The sponsor and product owner have decided to stop the initiative. Several developers argue that 'two more sprints' would prove the idea. What should the project manager do?
options: Support the developers' request for two more sprints, since stopping now would waste the investment already made
Close the initiative quietly and reassign the team, since the result reflects poorly on the sponsor's original decision
Treat the result as validated learning: record what was tested and learned, close the work properly, and release the team
Have the team pivot to a new product idea using the remaining budget, without first involving the sponsor or product owner
hint: The success criteria were agreed before the experiments began — what does that make of the outcome?
why: The experiments did their job: they tested a risky assumption cheaply and produced a clear answer against thresholds agreed in advance. The accountable decision makers have chosen to stop, so the project manager should support that decision, capture and share what was learned (about customers, channels and the technology), close the work properly, and release the team. Continuing because of money already spent is the sunk-cost fallacy, hiding the result wastes the learning, and pivoting without the sponsor and product owner bypasses governance.
how: When agreed evidence shows an idea will not deliver value, stop early, capture the learning openly, and close properly; money already spent is not a reason to continue.
optionNotes: Incorrect — Past spending is a sunk cost; the agreed evidence says further sprints are unlikely to create value.
Incorrect — Closing quietly throws away valuable learning and implies that a well-run experiment with a negative result is a failure.
Correct — It respects the decision makers, preserves the learning for the organization, and closes the effort cleanly.
Incorrect — Redirecting funds to a new idea without the sponsor and product owner bypasses governance and value decisions.
deepDive: The book acknowledges that every project can produce suboptimal outcomes and that experimental work is a deliberate investment in an uncertain result. Setting explicit success thresholds before experiments, sometimes called kill criteria, makes stopping a rational decision rather than a political one. Early termination is a legitimate closure path: document the state of the work, archive the learning, close contracts, and release resources. Agile and lean startup practice treats a disproved hypothesis as validated learning that saves the organization from larger losses.

topic: Open backlog items at project closure
source: ECO 2026 · Process Task 10 · Formal transfer of open items to the receiving owner at closure
question: A hybrid project delivering a citizen-services portal for a province has met every acceptance criterion in its charter, and the product owner has accepted the final release. Three low-priority enhancement stories remain in the product backlog. The sponsor wants to close the project this month. The operations manager who will own the portal is willing to consider the stories for a future release but has not yet received any information about them. What should the project manager do before closing?
options: Keep the project open until the three stories are delivered, because closing with open backlog items leaves scope incomplete
Formally hand the stories and their context to the operations manager, and record the transfer in the closure report
Delete the three stories from the backlog, since they were never part of the charter's agreed acceptance criteria
Ask the team to complete the three stories in one final unplanned sprint before closing, to leave a clean backlog
hint: The project's agreed scope is done; what should happen to the work that is left so that nothing gets lost?
why: The charter's acceptance criteria are met and the product owner has accepted the release, so the project can close. Remaining low-priority ideas are not unfinished project scope; they belong to the product, whose future owner is the operations manager. Handing them over with their context and recording the transfer ensures they are neither lost nor used as a reason to keep the project open, and it gives the operations manager what is needed to decide their future.
how: At closure, remaining backlog items that sit outside the accepted scope should be formally transferred to the product or operations owner, with the transfer documented, rather than deleted or used to extend the project.
optionNotes: Incorrect — The accepted scope is complete; keeping the project open for optional enhancements wastes resources and delays closure.
Correct — A documented handover lets the product's new owner decide on the stories and keeps the closure record complete.
Incorrect — Deleting the stories discards ideas the operations manager wants to consider and loses useful product knowledge.
Incorrect — An unplanned extra sprint adds unapproved work and cost; the product owner and sponsor have already accepted the outcome.
deepDive: In agile and hybrid work the product backlog belongs to the product, not the project, so it usually outlives the project and moves to the product or operations owner. Project closure confirms that agreed acceptance criteria are met, transfers ownership of deliverables and open items, and records the outcome in the final report. Leaving items undocumented creates confusion about what was promised, while extending the project for low-value work is a form of gold plating. The exam favors formal, documented handovers over informal or unilateral choices.
